s: Almost entirely supported and passive; nothing is held by muscle.
Avoids deep flexion and loaded rotation; built around gentle extension.
Breath-linked movement with short holds and frequent salutations.
Built for the kapha hours after waking, when the body is heavy and cold.
Built to close the day; no strong backbends, no heating breath.
Cooling and non-competitive; built for heat, irritability and the summer months.
Few shapes held for minutes, targeting connective tissue rather than muscle.
Fully supported shapes; nothing held by muscular effort.
Heating and stimulating; built to lift heaviness and inertia.
Longer static holds, classical shapes, little flowing.
Precise alignment with props, held long enough to correct.
Slow, grounding and warm; built to settle a scattered or anxious system.
Twists and gentle compression, taken well away from meals.
Weighted toward holds, core and arm balances.
Weighted toward long holds in folds and hip openers.
An arm balance with one leg behind the head and the other extended straight up.
Crow with the arms straight and the knees high in the armpits. Considerably harder than bent-arm crow and often confused with it.
Knees resting on the upper arms with the feet lifting. The first arm balance most practitioners achieve, and more about weight shift than strength.
Lowering from crow into tripod headstand and back. A controlled strength transition, not a drop.
Crow lowering the crown lightly to the floor as preparation for tripod headstand.
A side arm balance with one leg behind the head. Balance, rotation and extreme hip range together.
Legs threaded around one arm and extended sideways while the elbows bend. Named for the sage born with eight bends in his body.
One leg hooked over the upper arm with the body lifting on the hands.
Seated on the hands with both legs extending forward and up. Requires open hamstrings as much as arm strength.
One shin hooked across the upper arms with the other leg extending straight back. A hip opener and an arm balance at the same time.
A deeply twisted arm balance with one foot hooked over the opposite arm. One of the more advanced rotational balances.
A twisted arm balance with one foot hooked across the opposite arm and the other leg extended.
An arm balance with one leg forward and straight and the other back, like a hurdler mid-stride.
Crane Pose with one leg lifted. Halving the base doubles the demand on the supporting side and exposes any left-to-right imbalance immediately.

s: Peacock pose with the legs in lotus. Adds the knee demand of lotus to an already extreme wrist load.
Balanced horizontally on the elbows pressed into the belly. Classically said to digest even the most difficult food, and brutal on the wrists.
Arms threaded through a lotus and the body lifted. Demands full lotus before the balance can even be attempted.
Arms threaded through a lotus and the whole body rocking or balancing. From the Ashtanga primary series.
A twisted arm balance with the legs extended in opposite directions.
in: Sage Koundinya I (Eka Pada Koundinyasana I)

s: An open-legged arm balance with one leg forward over the arm and one extended back.
in: Sage Koundinya II (Eka Pada Koundinyasana II)

s: A side plank on one hand with the body in a single line. Builds lateral core strength that plank alone does not reach.
A forearm balance with the legs in lotus folded toward the head.
Lifting the whole lotus-seated body clear of the floor. A pure strength lift with no momentum available.
Legs hooked over the shoulders with the feet crossed in front. A compact, compressed arm balance from the Ashtanga primary series.
A twisted arm balance with both knees resting on one upper arm. Rotation and balance combined, and a common gateway to the harder balances.
Side plank with the top leg lifted or caught at the toe. Adds hamstring length and a balance demand to the side hold.
Side crow with the legs extending straight rather than stacked.
Crow with one leg extending straight back. Requires real core control to avoid collapsing forward.
Lifting the whole crossed-legged body clear of the floor on the hands. The closing lift of the Ashtanga series and a pure test of core and shoulder strength.
The closing lift of the Ashtanga sequence, held for twenty-five breaths in the traditional count.
Both legs hooked over the upper arms with the feet crossed. The compressed precursor to firefly.
The full cobra with the arms straight, the head reaching back and the feet approaching the crown.
Lying prone, ankles caught in the hands, chest and thighs lifting into a bow. Strong compression of the low back and full opening of the front.

Bow Pose practised with the wall as a reference. The wall removes the fear of falling and lets the alignment be felt rather than guessed, which is how the shape should be learned before it is held alone.
Bow Pose taken with a block under the supporting hand or beneath the seat. The prop shortens the distance to the floor so the spine can stay long instead of rounding to reach it.
Bow pose taken until the feet touch the crown.
in: Bow with Feet to Head (Ganda Bherundasana (bow))

s: Bow approached with a strap around the ankles. Lets the chest open before the shoulders can reach.
Feet planted and hips lifting with the shoulders rolled beneath. The entry backbend and a safe preparation for wheel.

s: Rolling the spine up and down from a bridge one vertebra at a time.
Bridge with a block squeezed between the thighs so the adductors and glutes engage together.
in: Bridge with Block Between Thighs (Setu Bandha (thigh block))

s: Bridge with the hands clasped beneath the body and the shoulders rolling under.
A standing chest opener with the arms bent at ninety degrees and the elbows drawing back.
Kneeling and arching back with hands reaching for the heels. Opens the whole front body and is famously destabilising emotionally.

s: An inverted staff backbend on the forearms with one leg lifted to vertical.
in: Eka Pada Viparita Dandasana (Eka Pada Viparita Dandasana)

s: Reclined with the chest lifting and the crown resting lightly on the floor. The classical counterpose to shoulderstand.
